name: Cameroon
summary: Formerly German Kamerun, divided between France and Britain after 1919; the French part became independent in 1960 and joined the southern British part in 1961.

knownFor.label: “Africa in miniature”
knownFor.note: Deserts, savanna, rainforest and coast in one country.

location.value: Central Africa on the Gulf of Guinea; about 475,442 km².

terrain.value: Coastal plain, rainforest, the Cameroon range highlands and savanna.

climate.value: Tropical along the coast and in the south, and semi-arid in the north near Lake Chad.

disasters.value: The Lake Nyos gas disaster (1986) killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.

urbanisation.value: Douala is the largest city and economic capital; Yaoundé is the capital.

migration.value: Hosts about 278,000 refugees from the Central African Republic and 127,000 from Nigeria (2025).

economicBase.value: Oil, farming (cocoa, coffee, bananas) and timber.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country, with large gaps between regions.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

keyRulers.value: Ahmadou Ahidjo (first president). Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: The president has ruled since 1982, with elections that critics say were unfair.

institutions.value: A National Assembly and Senate, though power is concentrated in the presidency.

stability.value: Protests from November 2016 became an armed conflict in 2017 (the Anglophone crisis); Boko Haram attacks in the north.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A national army that fights Boko Haram in the north and separatists in the west.

majorWars.value: The Anglophone crisis, a conflict between the army and separatists, began in 2016.

territoryChange.value: Southern Cameroons federated with Cameroon in 1961; Nigeria handed over Bakassi (2006–08).

alliancesRivals.value: Foreign policy closely follows France, a key defence partner.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Universities at Yaoundé and Buea, and a bilingual school system.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Camrail rail service and road networks; only 6.6% of roads are tarred.

languageWriting.value: French and English are official; about 250 native languages.

artsArchitecture.value: The Bamum script (1896) is a notable tradition.

sharedIdentity.value: Divisions between French- and English-speaking regions.

dailyLife.value: Many families eat ndolé (bitterleaf stew) and fufu (a starchy dough).

neighbours.value: Nigeria, Chad, Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity and Islam are the main faiths, alongside traditional beliefs.

colonisation.value: A German colony from 1884, then French and British mandates after the First World War.

riseSignals.value: Independence in 1960 (French Cameroon) and 1961 (British Southern Cameroons).

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Cameroon continues as an independent state.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
